overview.intro: A quadratic equation is the simplest equation that can have two answers, and the whole chapter is about finding them and understanding what they look like. Three tools do the work: factorisation when the roots are friendly, the quadratic formula when they are not, and the discriminant when the question is not asking for the roots at all but only what kind they are. The relations between roots and coefficients then replace the roots with sums and products, which is how examiners write questions that look impossible until you notice you never need the roots themselves.

learningOutcomes: Solve a quadratic equation by factorisation, by completing the square and by the quadratic formula.
Compute the discriminant and state the nature of the roots without solving the equation.
Use the relations between roots and coefficients to form and solve symmetric root problems.
Construct a quadratic equation whose roots are given, including reciprocal and shifted roots.
Translate a word problem into a quadratic equation, solve it and reject the root that the context forbids.

learn.title: Three ways to find the roots

blocks.text: Every quadratic equation is first written in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0, and dividing through by a puts the leading coefficient at one. Factorisation then looks for two numbers that multiply to the constant and add to the middle coefficient, and it fails gracefully when the roots are irrational or fractional — the formula takes over. The quadratic formula is nothing more than completing the square on the general equation: move c, divide by a, add (b/2a)² to both sides, collapse the left into a perfect square, and take the square root. That derivation is worth reproducing in an examination, because the method marks for completing the square are separate from the formula itself. Over the real numbers the formula always gives an answer once complex numbers are admitted, which is historically why the complex numbers were invented.

items: Standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0; the coefficient a must never be zero.
Factorisation works when the roots are rational: find p and q with p + q = b/a and pq = c/a.
Completing the square: x² + (b/a)x = −c/a, then add (b/2a)² to both sides.
Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a — the same for every quadratic, ever.
Check each root by substitution before writing the answer; one arithmetic slip halves the marks.

items.note: Two numbers adding to −5 and multiplying to +6 are −2 and −3.
Identify a = 2, b = −4, c = −6, compute D = 64, then substitute into the formula.

learn.title: The discriminant and the nature of roots

blocks.text: The discriminant D = b² − 4ac is the part of the quadratic formula under the square root, so it alone decides what kind of roots an equation has. If D is positive the square root is a real non-zero number and the ± sign gives two distinct real roots; if D is zero the roots coincide; if D is negative no real square root exists and the two roots form a complex conjugate pair. When the coefficients are rational, a further refinement applies: D is a perfect square if and only if the roots are rational, which is how a question can ask about rationality without asking for the roots. Because D is a single expression, it is also cheap to manipulate: to make a quadratic have equal roots for every value of a parameter, solve D = 0 for that parameter in one line.

items: D = b² − 4ac with the coefficients taken after dividing through so that a ≠ 0.
D > 0: two distinct real roots; D = 0: two equal real roots; D < 0: non-real complex conjugate roots.
Rational coefficients plus D a perfect square is exactly the condition for rational roots.
Non-real roots always appear as a conjugate pair a + ib and a − ib.
Setting D = 0 is the standard way to find a parameter value that makes roots equal.

items.text: x² − 6x + 9 = 0 has D = 36 − 36 = 0, so the root x = 3 occurs twice
items.note: A vanishing discriminant marks a perfect-square trinomial.

items.text: x² + x + 1 = 0 has D = 1 − 4 = −3 < 0, so no real roots exist
items.note: A negative D sends both roots off the real line into the complex plane.
Substitute a = 2, b = −4, c = 2 without simplifying the equation first.

items.text: For kx² + 4x + 1 = 0 to have no real roots, 16 − 4k < 0, so k > 4
items.note: Apply D < 0 to the parameter and solve the resulting linear inequality.

learn.title: Roots and coefficients: sums and products

blocks.text: For ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots α and β, the two relations α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a are the heart of the second half of the chapter, because they let a question about roots be answered without finding them. If a problem asks about α² + β², or 1/α + 1/β, or α³ + β³, the expression is rewritten in terms of the sum and the product — the identity α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ being the first one to reach for. The relations also run backwards: given any two numbers, the equation having them as roots is x² − (sum)x + product = 0, and once a is chosen the equation follows by clearing fractions. Reciprocal roots force the product to one, which with αβ = c/a means a = c; roots that are negatives of each other force the sum to zero, meaning b = 0.

items: α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a for the equation ax² + bx + c = 0.
α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ; use it before touching any squares.
1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/αβ and α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β).
Equation from roots: x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0, multiplied by a to clear fractions.
Reciprocal roots ⇔ αβ = 1 ⇔ a = c; opposite roots ⇔ α + β = 0 ⇔ b = 0.

items.text: If α + β = 5 and αβ = 6, then α² + β² = 25 − 12 = 13
items.note: Apply the identity instead of finding 2 and 3 individually.

items.text: Roots 2 and −2 give x² − 0·x − 4 = 0, i.e. x² − 4 = 0
items.note: Sum zero kills the linear term; the product gives the constant.

blocks.text: The last lesson is about translation: taking a sentence and producing an equation. Almost every applied quadratic follows one of two patterns — a quantity split into parts, where the parts multiply to a constant, or a rate and time relationship, where work adds as reciprocals. Once the equation exists the algebra is routine, but the answer is not: a quadratic normally returns two roots and a real problem returns one, so the second root is rejected only after the reason is stated. Speed problems reject a negative time, geometry problems reject a negative length, and reciprocal-time problems reject any root that makes a denominator zero. Writing the rejection down is part of the answer — an unstated rejection looks like an oversight.

items: Let the unknown be the smallest quantity the problem speaks of, then write everything else against it.
Work problems: add the rates, not the times — 1/x + 1/(x + 10) = 1/12.
Geometry problems: side lengths must be positive, so a negative root dies on contact.
Check the surviving root by substituting it back into the original sentence.
State why the second root is rejected; the reason carries a mark of its own.

items.text: A does a job in 10 days more than B; together they finish in 12 days
items.note: 1/x + 1/(x + 10) = 1/12 leads to x² − 14x − 120 = 0 with x = 20, so B takes 20 days and A takes 30.

items.text: Two numbers differ by 3 and their product is 40: x(x + 3) = 40 → x² + 3x − 40 = 0
items.note: Factorising gives (x + 8)(x − 5) = 0; the negative root is rejected for a positive number, giving 5 and 8.

keyPoints: Standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0, precedes every method of solution.
Factorisation handles rational roots; the quadratic formula handles all others.
Completing the square derives the formula and earns its own method marks.
D = b² − 4ac: positive means distinct real roots, zero means a repeated root, negative means a conjugate pair.
Rational roots require rational coefficients and a discriminant that is a perfect square.
α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a answer symmetric questions without finding the roots.
α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ is the identity that most root questions require.
The equation with given roots α and β is x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0.
Reciprocal roots force a = c; opposite roots force b = 0.
Applied problems reject one root, and the rejection must be stated with its reason.
examFocus: Write a, b and c explicitly before substituting into the formula; sign slips on b are the most common lost mark.
For nature-of-roots questions, quote the discriminant condition alongside the conclusion — both lines are marked.
Roots-and-coefficients questions are answered with identities: state α + β and αβ first, then rewrite the expression.
In word problems, define the variable in words with units, and give the final answer as a sentence, not just a number.

questions.prompt: The discriminant of 2x² − 4x + 2 = 0 shows that its roots are:
questions.explanation: D = (−4)² − 4(2)(2) = 16 − 16 = 0, and a zero discriminant means two equal real roots — in fact x = 2 twice.

questions.prompt: The sum of the roots of 3x² − 5x + 2 = 0 is:
questions.explanation: α + β = −b/a = −(−5)/3 = 5/3, positive because the middle coefficient is negative.

questions.prompt: The roots of the equation x² + 4 = 0 are:
questions.explanation: x² = −4 gives x = ±2i: the discriminant is −16, so both roots lie off the real axis and are conjugates of each other.

questions.prompt: For an equation with integer coefficients to have rational roots, its discriminant must be:
questions.explanation: The formula divides √D by 2a, so the roots are rational exactly when √D is rational — for integers, when D is a perfect square.

questions.prompt: The condition for ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0) to have equal roots is that the discriminant ______ equals zero.
questions.explanation: Setting b² − 4ac = 0 makes the ± term vanish, collapsing both roots onto the single value −b/2a.

questions.prompt: The product of the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 is ______ .
questions.explanation: From the factorisation a(x − α)(x − β), the constant term is aαβ, so αβ = c/a.

questions.prompt: State the relations between the coefficients and the roots of a quadratic equation, and the equation built from them.
questions.answer: For ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots α and β: α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. Conversely, the equation whose roots are α and β is x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0, which may be multiplied through by any non-zero constant.
questions.explanation: These two lines replace root-finding in every symmetric question; they come straight from expanding a(x − α)(x − β).

questions.prompt: State the nature of the roots of a quadratic equation when its discriminant is negative.
questions.answer: There are no real roots: the pair of roots is non-real and complex conjugate, of the form a + ib and a − ib with b ≠ 0. The square root of the negative discriminant introduces i, and conjugacy follows because the coefficients remain real.
questions.explanation: A negative discriminant blocks the real square root, and complex numbers restore it with the ± pair, which are conjugates of each other.

questions.prompt: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 by factorisation and verify your answer with the relations between roots and coefficients.
questions.answer: The factorisation is (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 because −2 and −3 add to −5 and multiply to +6, giving roots 2 and 3. Check: α + β = 2 + 3 = 5, which equals −b/a = −(−5)/1, and αβ = 2 × 3 = 6, which equals c/a = 6/1. Both relations confirm the roots.
questions.explanation: Factorise by finding the pair matching b and c, then verify through both coefficient relations rather than by substitution alone — the question asks for the verification explicitly.

questions.prompt: A job is done by A alone in 10 days more than B alone, and together they finish it in 12 days. Find the time each takes alone.
questions.answer: Let B take x days, so A takes x + 10. Their combined rate is 1/x + 1/(x + 10) = 1/12. Multiplying by 12x(x + 10) gives 12(x + 10) + 12x = x(x + 10), that is x² − 14x − 120 = 0, with roots x = (14 ± √(196 + 480))/2 = (14 ± 26)/2, so x = 20 or x = −10. Time cannot be negative, so x = 20: B takes 20 days and A takes 30 days. Together 1/20 + 1/30 = 5/60 = 1/12, matching the given 12 days.
questions.explanation: Add rates rather than times, clear the denominators to reach a standard quadratic, and reject the negative root with a stated reason before verifying the answer against the original condition.
